subsections: Horizontal distribution - isotherms in January vs July, land-sea contrast

accepted.s: With reference to the January isotherms in the Northern Hemisphere, which one of the following is correct?
o: They bend equatorward over both land and oceans because January is a winter month.
They run exactly along the parallels because land and oceans have equal temperatures.
They bend poleward over land and equatorward over oceans because land remains warmer than oceans.
They bend equatorward over land and poleward over oceans because oceans are warmer than land.
accepted.x: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend equatorward over colder landmasses and poleward over relatively warmer oceans.
accepted.tq: Use the land-sea contrast to distinguish the direction of the January bends.
accepted.sec: Horizontal distribution - isotherms in January vs July, land-sea contrast

accepted.s: In July, the isotherms of the Northern Hemisphere generally bend poleward over landmasses because
o: water heats faster than land during summer.
oceans are always warmer than land in July.
land heats faster than water during summer.
land receives no insolation during July.
accepted.x: Land heats more rapidly than water, so summer temperatures over continents are relatively higher and the isotherms bend poleward over land.
accepted.tq: Apply the faster heating of land to identify the summer isotherm pattern.
accepted.sec: Horizontal distribution - isotherms in January vs July, land-sea contrast

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding isotherms:
1. Isotherms join places having equal temperature.
2. They generally run east-west, parallel to latitudes.
3. They are more regular in the Southern Hemisphere because it has a greater oceanic area.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Isotherms connect places of equal temperature, generally follow an east-west direction, and are more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.
accepted.tq: Check each definition, orientation and hemispheric comparison separately.
accepted.sec: Horizontal distribution - isotherms in January vs July, land-sea contrast

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the winter temperature pattern in India?
o: Temperature rises from north to south only in coastal areas.
Temperature remains uniform from north to south because the 20°C isotherm is straight.
Temperature generally rises from north to south.
Temperature generally falls from north to south because the south is farther from the Equator.
accepted.x: During Indian winter, temperature generally increases from north to south, consistent with the southward decrease in latitude.
accepted.tq: Use the north-south temperature trend rather than the location of one isotherm alone.
accepted.sec: Horizontal distribution - isotherms in January vs July, land-sea contrast

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Coastal areas — continental climate with a large annual range
Northern interiors — maritime climate with mild summers and winters
Coastal areas — maritime climate with a small annual range
Northern interiors — equable climate throughout the year
accepted.x: The sea moderates temperature in coastal areas, producing an equable or maritime climate with a small annual range.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the maritime and continental effects of location.
accepted.sec: Annual and diurnal range - continental vs maritime, latitude of minimum range, clear vs cloudy nights

accepted.s: The largest annual range of temperature is generally found in
o: continental interiors of high latitudes such as Siberia
maritime regions of the Southern Hemisphere
equatorial coastal regions
islands near the Equator
accepted.x: Continental interiors at high latitudes experience very hot summers and very cold winters, producing a large annual range; Siberia is a standard example.
accepted.tq: Combine continentality with high latitude to locate the maximum annual range.
accepted.sec: Annual and diurnal range - continental vs maritime, latitude of minimum range, clear vs cloudy nights

accepted.s: At which latitude is the minimum annual range of temperature generally observed?
o: At 66½° north latitude
At the Equator
At the poles
At 23½° north latitude
accepted.x: The annual range is generally minimum at the Equator because seasonal changes in solar altitude and day length are small.
accepted.tq: Recall the latitude associated with the minimum annual range.
accepted.sec: Annual and diurnal range - continental vs maritime, latitude of minimum range, clear vs cloudy nights

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements about diurnal temperature range in Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: The coast and Rayalaseema have identical diurnal ranges.
Rayalaseema generally has a higher diurnal range than the coast.
The coast generally has a higher diurnal range than Rayalaseema.
The diurnal range is lowest in all interior areas of Andhra Pradesh.
accepted.x: The maritime influence reduces the coastal diurnal range, whereas the interior Rayalaseema region generally has a higher range.
accepted.tq: Compare coastal moderation with interior continental conditions.
accepted.sec: Annual and diurnal range - continental vs maritime, latitude of minimum range, clear vs cloudy nights

accepted.s: The winter diurnal range of temperature in north-western India is approximately
accepted.x: The winter diurnal range in north-western India is about 14–18°C.
accepted.tq: Identify the exact range rather than selecting the nearest broad estimate.
accepted.sec: Annual and diurnal range - continental vs maritime, latitude of minimum range, clear vs cloudy nights

accepted.s: Clear nights are generally colder than cloudy nights because clear skies
o: increase incoming short-wave radiation at night.
prevent the Earth from emitting long-wave radiation.
permit greater loss of heat by terrestrial radiation.
create strong convection from the upper atmosphere.
accepted.x: Clear skies allow greater radiational loss of heat from the Earth, whereas clouds send some outgoing heat back toward the surface.
accepted.tq: Link night-time temperature to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
accepted.sec: Annual and diurnal range - continental vs maritime, latitude of minimum range, clear vs cloudy nights

accepted.s: The normal environmental lapse rate is approximately
o: 1°C per 165 m
1°C per 65 m
1°C per 365 m
1°C per 265 m
accepted.x: The normal lapse rate is 6.5°C per kilometre, equivalent to approximately 1°C per 165 metres.
accepted.tq: Convert the standard lapse rate into its metre equivalent.
accepted.sec: Vertical distribution - normal lapse rate and why temperature falls with height

accepted.s: The normal lapse rate of temperature in the troposphere is approximately
o: 5.0°C per km
9.8°C per km
6.5°C per km
3.5°C per km
accepted.x: Under normal conditions, temperature decreases at about 6.5°C for every kilometre increase in height.
accepted.tq: Recall the standard numerical value of the lapse rate.
accepted.sec: Vertical distribution - normal lapse rate and why temperature falls with height

accepted.s: Why does temperature normally decrease with increasing altitude?
o: Higher air receives more long-wave radiation from the Sun.
The ground heats the air from below, while higher air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust.
The Earth stops emitting radiation above the lower atmosphere.
The atmosphere is heated mainly from above by direct solar radiation.
accepted.x: The ground heats the atmosphere from below. At higher levels the air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.
accepted.tq: Identify the heating source and the properties of higher air.
accepted.sec: Vertical distribution - normal lapse rate and why temperature falls with height

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the radiation processes involved in atmospheric heating?
o: The Sun emits long-wave radiation and the Earth re-emits short-wave radiation.
The Sun emits short-wave radiation and the Earth re-emits long-wave infrared radiation.
Both the Sun and the Earth emit only short-wave radiation.
Both the Sun and the Earth emit only long-wave radiation.
accepted.x: Solar radiation is primarily short-wave, while the Earth re-emits absorbed energy as long-wave infrared radiation.
accepted.tq: Avoid the common reversal of solar and terrestrial radiation.
accepted.sec: Vertical distribution - normal lapse rate and why temperature falls with height

accepted.s: The long-wave infrared radiation re-emitted by the Earth lies approximately in the range of
accepted.x: Earth's outgoing long-wave infrared radiation is approximately in the 8,000–25,000 nanometre range.
accepted.tq: Recall the radiation wavelength range stated for terrestrial emission.
accepted.sec: Vertical distribution - normal lapse rate and why temperature falls with height

accepted.s:
Which of the following factors affect the amount of insolation received at a place?
1. Angle of the Sun's rays
2. Length of the day
3. Transparency of the atmosphere
4. Slope and aspect of the land
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
accepted.x: The angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, atmospheric transparency, and slope and aspect of land all influence insolation.
accepted.tq: Test the complete list of controlling factors rather than one isolated cause.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: Vertical rays of the Sun produce greater heating because they
o: are always blocked by clouds and dust.
travel through a thicker atmosphere and cover a larger area.
heat a smaller surface area with more concentrated energy.
occur only over the poles.
accepted.x: Vertical rays concentrate solar energy over a smaller area, producing greater heating than oblique rays.
accepted.tq: Apply the relationship between ray angle, concentration and heating.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the Earth's aphelion?
o: Around 4 July at 152 million km
Around 3 January at 147 million km
Around 21 March at 150 million km
Around 23 September at 147 million km
accepted.x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.
accepted.tq: Use the paired contrast between perihelion and aphelion.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: Which region generally receives the maximum insolation?
o: The equatorial region, because cloud cover is greatest there
The subtropical deserts, because they have relatively little cloud cover
Oceanic regions at all latitudes, because water absorbs all radiation
The polar regions, because summer days are long
accepted.x: Maximum insolation is generally received in subtropical deserts, where cloud cover is low; it is not necessarily maximum at the Equator.
accepted.tq: Distinguish maximum received insolation from annual insolation and from day length.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements about the latitudinal distribution of insolation is correct?
o: Insolation is always higher over oceans than continents at the same latitude.
Insolation generally decreases towards the poles and is higher over continents than oceans at the same latitude.
Insolation increases continuously from the Equator to the poles.
The poles receive the maximum annual insolation because of long summer days.
accepted.x: Insolation generally declines towards the poles and, at the same latitude, is higher over continents than oceans. Long polar summer days do not give the poles maximum annual insolation.
accepted.tq: Check both the poleward trend and the land-sea comparison.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes maximum annual insolation from maximum instantaneous insolation?
o: The Equator receives the most annual insolation, while subtropical deserts generally receive the maximum insolation because of low cloud cover.
The Equator and the poles receive equal annual insolation.
The poles receive the most annual insolation, while the Equator receives the least.
Subtropical deserts receive the least annual insolation because they are dry.
accepted.x: The Equator receives the most annual insolation, whereas maximum insolation at a given time or region is associated with the relatively cloudless subtropical deserts.
accepted.tq: Separate the annual total from the regional maximum caused by cloud conditions.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: An urban heat island is primarily produced because
o: cities receive no long-wave radiation at night.
rural vegetation reflects all incoming radiation toward cities.
urban areas are always located at lower latitudes than rural areas.
concrete and asphalt store heat and make cities warmer than surrounding rural areas.
accepted.x: Concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, causing urban areas to be warmer than their rural surroundings.
accepted.tq: Identify the physical surface property responsible for the urban-rural temperature contrast.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: The reported urban heat-island intensity of Hyderabad is approximately
accepted.x: Hyderabad's reported urban heat-island intensity is approximately 5.74–6.82°C.
accepted.tq: Recall the exact two-ended range of the city-specific measurement.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: Data centres were reported to add approximately how much to land-surface temperature within 10 km?
accepted.x: Data centres were reported to add approximately 2°C to land-surface temperature within a 10-kilometre radius.
accepted.tq: Match the magnitude with the specified spatial radius.
accepted.sec: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

accepted.s: Temperature inversion refers to a condition in which
o: temperature remains constant at all heights.
temperature rises with height instead of falling.
temperature falls more rapidly with height than under normal conditions.
temperature rises only over oceans during summer.
accepted.x: During an inversion, the normal lapse relationship is reversed and temperature increases with height.
accepted.tq: Use the reversal of the normal lapse rate as the defining feature.
accepted.sec: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

accepted.s: Which combination of conditions is most favourable for the development of a temperature inversion?
o: Short summer nights, cloudy skies, strong winds and humid air
Long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air and snow cover
Long summer days, heavy rainfall, strong convection and moist air
Cloudy nights, strong turbulence and high surface temperatures
accepted.x: Long winter nights, clear skies, calm and dry air, and snow cover favour rapid surface cooling and inversion formation.
accepted.tq: Select the complete set of inversion-producing conditions.
accepted.sec: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

accepted.s: In a valley inversion, the valley floor is colder than the slopes because
o: warm air flows downslope and accumulates at the valley floor.
the valley floor is always nearer to the Sun.
cold air drains downslope and settles in the valley.
the slopes receive no solar radiation in winter.
accepted.x: Cold, dense air flows downslope and accumulates in valleys, producing frost pockets while the slopes remain relatively warmer.
accepted.tq: Follow the movement of dense cold air to determine the colder location.
accepted.sec: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Frontal inversion — association with a frontal boundary
Valley inversion — downslope drainage of cold air
Surface or radiation inversion — night-time cooling of the ground
Stratosphere — absence of any inversion condition
accepted.x: The stratosphere is a permanent inversion layer, so it is incorrect to associate it with the absence of inversion.
accepted.tq: Find the single reversed or denied relationship in the list.
accepted.sec: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

accepted.s: A practical agricultural adaptation to valley inversion is to locate orchards and plantations on upper slopes because
o: upper slopes receive no radiation during clear nights.
upper slopes are generally warmer than valley floors during inversion.
cold air rises naturally from valleys to slopes.
valley floors always have deeper soils and warmer air.
accepted.x: Cold air settles on valley floors during an inversion, making upper slopes relatively warmer and more suitable for orchards and plantations.
accepted.tq: Apply the frost-pocket concept to a land-use decision.
accepted.sec: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

accepted.s:
Which of the following are effects of temperature inversion?
1. Fog
2. Frost
3. Smog
4. Trapping of pollutants in the planetary boundary layer
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
accepted.x: Inversions can produce fog, frost and smog and can trap pollutants within the planetary boundary layer.
accepted.tq: Recognise the common atmospheric and pollution effects as one complete group.
accepted.sec: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

accepted.s: Heavy moisture and fog on winter mornings in North India are commonly associated with
o: maximum insolation at the surface during the night
permanent advection of hot desert air
a strong normal lapse rate and intense upward convection
temperature inversion near the surface
accepted.x: Surface temperature inversion, together with heavy moisture, commonly produces dense winter fog in North India.
accepted.tq: Connect the regional weather phenomenon with the relevant atmospheric process.
accepted.sec: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

accepted.s: The thermal equator is best defined as the
o: line joining places of highest mean temperature, generally lying north of the geographical Equator.
boundary between the tropical and polar zones, fixed at 23½° latitude.
line joining the coldest places in both hemispheres.
geographical Equator, which never shifts seasonally.
accepted.x: The thermal equator is the line of highest mean temperature. It lies mostly north of the geographical Equator and shifts with the apparent movement of the Sun.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the shifting thermal equator from the fixed geographical Equator.
accepted.sec: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places

accepted.s:
Assertion (A): The thermal equator shifts during the year.
Reason (R): It follows the apparent seasonal movement of the Sun.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
accepted.x: Both statements are true, and the seasonal apparent movement of the Sun causes the line of highest mean temperature to shift.
accepted.tq: Test whether the reason directly accounts for the seasonal movement.
accepted.sec: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places

accepted.s: According to the reported figures for Chennai, which change occurred between 2014 and 2024?
o: Vegetation increased from 10% to 25% and built-up area fell from 67% to 36%.
Vegetation fell from 25% to 10% and built-up area rose from 36% to 67%.
Vegetation and built-up area both remained unchanged.
Vegetation fell from 36% to 25% and built-up area rose from 10% to 67%.
accepted.x: Chennai's vegetation reportedly declined from 25% in 2014 to 10% in 2024, while built-up area increased from 36% to 67%.
accepted.tq: Track both directional changes and their exact percentages.
accepted.sec: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Dras — about −45°C recorded in 1908
Death Valley — −89.2°C
Vostok — 56.7°C
Lambasingi — −45°C recorded in 1908
accepted.x: Dras in Ladakh recorded approximately −45°C in 1908. Death Valley is associated with 56.7°C, while Vostok is associated with −89.2°C.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure place-temperature pair and eliminate swapped extremes.
accepted.sec: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places

accepted.s: The highest temperature among the following recorded extremes is associated with
o: Vostok, at −89.2°C
Lambasingi, at about 2°C
Death Valley, at 56.7°C
Dras, at −45°C
accepted.x: Death Valley recorded 56.7°C, the highest temperature among the listed world and regional extremes.
accepted.tq: Compare the signs and magnitudes before selecting the maximum.
accepted.sec: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs relating to Andhra Pradesh temperature extremes is correctly matched?
o: Rentachintala — hottest place, above 47°C
Lambasingi — hottest place, above 47°C
Rentachintala — coldest place, about 2°C
Lambasingi — coldest place, −45°C
accepted.x: Rentachintala in Palnadu is identified as the hottest place in Andhra Pradesh, with temperatures above 47°C.
accepted.tq: Separate the state’s hottest and coldest places before matching the figures.
accepted.sec: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places

accepted.s: Lambasingi, located in ASR district, is known as the ‘Kashmir of Andhra Pradesh’ because it is
o: the coldest place in the State, with temperatures of about 2°C.
the place with the highest urban heat-island intensity.
the hottest place in the State, with temperatures above 47°C.
situated on the thermal equator.
accepted.x: Lambasingi in ASR district is regarded as the coldest place in Andhra Pradesh, with temperatures of about 2°C, and is called the ‘Kashmir of AP’.
accepted.tq: Use the title and temperature figure together to identify the place.
accepted.sec: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places
